meeting_header:
Date: 2026-05-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ethan Kim (Redwood AE); Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE); Jordan Li (Redwood CSM); Priya Nair (Atlas VP Eng); Tom Harker (Atlas SRE); Lena Ortiz (Atlas Security); Markus Voss (Atlas Product)
summary: Post-incident review for edge cache stress that caused elevated 500s and degraded latency during a regional traffic spike. Discussed immediate mitigations (aggressive cache invalidation rollback, KV cache sizing), root cause hypotheses (cache hot-shard + mis-sized autoscale policy + prefix cache eviction behavior), and longer-term mitigations (workload-aware batching, regional fallback routing, SLO-driven autoscaling). Agreed next steps: patch config, replay in staging, schedule bench with Redwood SE, and share security artifacts for compliance review.
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Kim: Okay, thanks everyone for joining, we'll keep this to about 45 minutes, uh go through the incident timeline and then next steps. Priya, do you want to kick off with a quick run of what you saw?
[00:10] Priya Nair: Yeah sure, thanks Ethan. So on 2026-05-27 about 11:42 UTC we saw a sudden uptick in requests in EMEA region, traffic ~3x baseline, by 11:46 token generation latency spiked and then we started to see 5xxs go up to ~7%.
[00:30] Tom Harker: just to add, the 5xx were mostly inference timeouts on the edge pool, same model, we also saw large KV cache miss ratios and a bunch of evictions. I think some of our prefix cache keys were thrashing.
[00:47] Sofia Alvarez: (SE) when you say prefix thrash, do you mean the prefix cache eviction rate increased or that different shards were hot?
[00:55] Tom Harker: both, uh we had two hot shards and then the eviction churn caused async calls to hit backend more often and the runtime couldn't sustain the token throughput under our current autoscaler profile.
[01:10] Lena Ortiz: Security note — we also got a compliance alert about audit log gaps during the window. Not all request ids are present in our central audit store, likely because some proxies returned before logging finished.
[01:25] Jordan Li: (CSM) thanks Lena, we'll capture that as an action item, but first root cause. Ethan, do you have the Redwood telemetry handy?
[01:33] Ethan Kim: Yeah I pulled the per-model latency heatmap and KV cache metrics, attaching afterwards. Quick call-out: there was an unusual pattern at 11:44 where the runtime started fallbacking to a smaller model variant, which increased per-request token churn due to different tokenization; not sure if that made things worse or actually helped throughput in some slots.
[01:55] Priya Nair: We saw that, yes. The fallback seemed to trigger after the autoscaler hit max replicas for the pool and routing policy switched. But routing fallback was slightly mis-configured — it routed to a variant with a different sequence length expectation.
[02:12] Markus Voss: that mismatch caused lost cache hits because tokenization prefixing was different, so caches were less effective.
[02:20] Sofia Alvarez: okay that aligns with one of our hypotheses: 1) hot-shard on KV/prefix cache 2) autoscaler did not scale fast enough (policy thresholds too high) 3) fallback routing to incompatible variant amplified cache miss rate.
[02:36] Tom Harker: question — is the autoscaler relying on cpu/mem or token-aware qps? we had it on CPU.
[02:42] Sofia Alvarez: currently it's CPU+latency, not token-aware. We have an experimental token-aware policy that uses per-request token estimate, but it's not enabled for your dedicated pool.
[02:52] Priya Nair: We run a mix of short chat and long-document summarization. The long docs spike token lengths which is probably what pushed the runtime.
[03:03] Ethan Kim: Right. A couple of quick fixes that helped on your side were 1) rolling back a recent aggressive prefix invalidation rule and 2) bumping the autoscaler max replicas temporarily, both reduced 5xx.
[03:18] Priya Nair: Correct, we rolled those back at 12:10 and saw 5xx reduce to 1.2% in 20 minutes. But we want to avoid manual interventions going forward.
[03:28] Jordan Li: let's talk mitigations short-term vs long-term. Short-term is config tweaks and patch that's low risk. Long-term is runtime changes and routing rules.
[03:35] Sofia Alvarez: for short-term we propose: enable token-aware autoscale for the pool, add a cooldown so it scales earlier, and change fallback routing policy to prefer compatible variants only (model family and tokenizer match).
[03:50] Tom Harker: how invasive is that token-aware autoscale? we can't have weird scaling oscillations.
[03:55] Sofia Alvarez: it's tested internally; the main risk is false positives where a transient batch looks large, so we'd recommend smoothing window of 30s and a conservative multiplier. We'll provide a recommended config.
[04:08] Lena Ortiz: on the audit log issue, what's Redwood's guarantee on request-id propagation and audit logs when fallback happens?
[04:15] Ethan Kim: We do propagate request ids end-to-end normally; during the incident some proxies in the path returned early which caused missing entries. We're going to add a gating write to the audit stream for critical routes and surface any proxy-level timeouts in the console. Jordan will send the SOC2/KMS docs.
[04:31] Jordan Li: noted. I'll share the link to KMS integration docs and the team that owns audit pipeline, plus a contact for escalation.
[04:37] Priya Nair: also want to discuss pilot: hosted pilot with Redwood or dedicated pool? We need committed latency and isolation for peak retail hours.
[04:48] Ethan Kim: tradeoffs: hosted is faster to spin up and Redwood can route across regions, but dedicated gives you reserved capacity and more predictable tail latency. Given your peak variability, a small dedicated pool plus token-aware autoscale sounds like the right middle ground.
[05:03] Markus Voss: cost-wise can we cap burst? procurement will push back if costs spike.
[05:08] Ethan Kim: yes we can add budget caps and alerting per project, and also propose a burst policy that falls back to smaller model family under cost thresholds. That would degrade gracefully instead of failing hard.
[05:21] Tom Harker: one technical deep-dive: what's the KV cache eviction policy? We need to know how large the working set should be.
[05:28] Sofia Alvarez: current default is LRU per shard with a soft eviction threshold at 85% then hard at 95%, but for your mix we recommend tuning shard sizes and increasing the soft threshold to reduce churn; also consider hot-shard splitting.
[05:45] Priya Nair: hot-shard splitting sounds relevant, what's the work required?
[05:49] Sofia Alvarez: we can do online shard splitting, but it takes coordination: a short period of increased load during split, but we've automated it in platform — we'll provide a runbook.
[05:58] Lena Ortiz: from a security perspective, KMS rotations are monthly — does shard splitting affect key access patterns?
[06:05] Sofia Alvarez: no, it's purely logical partitioning, keys remain the same, KMS calls unaffected.
[06:11] Tom Harker: regarding telemetry — can Redwood expose per-shard miss rates and per-token latencies to our observability? we want to add these to our oncall dashboard.
[06:19] Ethan Kim: yes, we can push a Grafana dashboard feed and a Prometheus endpoint; we'll provide a starter dashboard.
[06:24] Markus Voss: a thing we worried about — degraded responses returning partial outputs during the fallback. Is there a way to enforce response completeness SLA?
[06:33] Sofia Alvarez: there's a per-request deadline in the runtime; we can increase internal tail timeout but that risks coupling user latency; better is to prefer compatible variants that preserve output shape, plus introduce a canary route that returns a deterministic fallback message rather than partial tokens.
[06:49] Priya Nair: agreed, deterministic fallback is better for product.
[06:52] Jordan Li: I'll add deterministic fallback to the pilot acceptance criteria.
[06:57] Tom Harker: what about stress-testing? we want to reproduce the 3x spike with the same token distribution.
[07:04] Sofia Alvarez: we recommend a staged replay: 1) replay on staging with same traces at 0.5x then 1x then 3x, 2) run a local bench with dedicated GPU to measure tail latency, 3) run a short live pilot with traffic mirroring. We'll help run steps 1 and 2.
[07:24] Priya Nair: timeline for that? we want results within two weeks.
[07:28] Ethan Kim: doable. We'll aim to deliver the config diff and staging replay plan by 2026-06-02, bench slot week of 2026-06-08.
[07:36] Lena Ortiz: compliance asks — can we get a statement about data residency and retention during the pilot? We need the retention window tied to our policy.
[07:43] Jordan Li: yes, Redwood provides configurable retention per-tenant; I'll include the retention SLA and sample retention config in the SOC2 pack we share.
[07:51] Priya Nair: another small thing: can we have a postmortem template? We want to capture blamelessly and share internally.
[07:57] Jordan Li: we have a template, I'll attach it.
[08:00] [crosstalk briefly]
[08:05] Mark us Voss: sorry, quick question - was there any indication of noisy neighbor from other tenants on the same node?
[08:11] Sofia Alvarez: we checked tenant isolation metrics — no cross-tenant CPU saturation, it appears workload skew within Atlas's own tenant caused hot shards.
[08:19] Tom Harker: what about prioritization of critical routes? we want an emergency routing that guarantees 99th p95 for our checkout path.
[08:26] Ethan Kim: we can tag routes with priority and reserve a small percentage of capacity; that requires config and a policy update, but it's doable.
[08:33] Priya Nair: please add that to the pilot scope as well.
[08:36] Sofia Alvarez: noted. We'll include route-priority config in the diff.
[08:40] Priya Nair: any concerns about changing fallback to compatible variants, might that reduce availability if those variants are overloaded?
[08:47] Sofia Alvarez: it's a balancing act; our suggested policy is prefer compatible but allow a secondary, cheaper variant under strict guardrails. Also add automatic KV-cache prewarm for the chosen variant when fallback occurs.
[08:59] Tom Harker: prewarm how long?
[09:02] Sofia Alvarez: usually 30-60s to load relevant kv entries, depends on working set size; prewarm is best-effort, not synchronous.
[09:10] Priya Nair: after these changes, how do we measure success?
[09:14] Ethan Kim: success criteria: reduce 5xx during similar spikes to <0.5%, maintain p95 latency under your target (250ms for API calls), no missing audit logs for critical routes, and no manual rollbacks for at least two high-traffic events.
[09:29] Priya Nair: sounds good.
[09:31] Jordan Li: quick recap of next steps — Sofia will share config diff and recommended autoscaler settings; Tom will share traces; Jordan will share SOC2/KMS/audit docs; Ethan will schedule bench; Priya will confirm pilot scope.
[09:46] Ethan Kim: perfect. Any other questions?
[09:49] Markus Voss: just one — can you share a short runbook for immediate mitigation if this happens again?
[09:54] Sofia Alvarez: yes, we'll write a 1-pager: rollback invalidation, bump autoscaler, enable token-aware policy, and apply route priority; publish in 24 hours.
[10:06] Priya Nair: thanks. If we get the config diff by Tuesday we can start staging tests Wednesday.
[10:12] Ethan Kim: great — we'll follow up with calendar invites. Thanks everyone.
[10:18] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription: occasional words mis-recognized (e.g., "shard" as "sharp" sometimes in internal logs), timestamps approximate, speaker overlap present. Attachments referenced: per-model latency heatmap (link), KV cache eviction logs (link), SOC2 & KMS docs (link).
